Under the federal Anti‑Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. § 1320a‑7b) and the Stark Law, any arrangement that induces or rewards referrals for Medicare Advantage services is prohibited unless it falls within a statutory safe harbor. Contracts should therefore contain an explicit “No Kickbacks” clause that prohibits the exchange of anything of value in return for patient referrals, including indirect incentives such as preferential scheduling or marketing support. The clause must specify that all remuneration is strictly tied to objective performance metrics (e.g., HEDIS measures) and not to individual patient volume. A separate “Safe‑Harbor Compliance” provision should require the parties to maintain documentation—such as written agreements, invoices, and audit trails—to demonstrate that any payments are made at fair market value for bona fide services rendered. The contract must also provide a mechanism for periodic review of remuneration structures by an independent third party to ensure continued compliance with the safe‑harbor requirements.

**Full‑Risk Capitation Governance**

In a full‑risk capitation arrangement, the insurer assumes financial risk for all covered beneficiaries, making accurate cost forecasting and risk adjustment essential. The contract should include a “Capitation Adjustment” clause that obliges the provider to submit quarterly claims data and demographic information in accordance with CMS’s Risk Adjustment Model (RAM) requirements. This provision must also require the provider to participate in any CMS‑approved quality improvement initiatives and to report HEDIS performance metrics on a timely basis. A “Performance‑Based Bonus” clause should be drafted to align incentives with quality outcomes, but it must expressly tie bonuses to objective thresholds that are not contingent upon patient volume or referral patterns. The contract should also contain an “Audit & Reconciliation” provision allowing the insurer to conduct annual audits of cost reports and to adjust capitation payments accordingly; any adjustments must be documented in writing and subject to dispute resolution procedures.

**Fraud, Waste, and Abuse Provisions**

The False Claims Act (FCA) imposes liability for knowingly submitting false or fraudulent claims. Contracts should therefore incorporate a “No Fraud” clause that requires the provider to certify, on an annual basis, that all claims submitted under the capitation agreement are accurate and truthful. A “Reporting Obligation” provision must mandate immediate notification of any suspected fraud, waste, or abuse to both CMS and the insurer’s compliance officer. Additionally, a “Co‑operative Investigation” clause should obligate the provider to cooperate with federal investigations, including providing access to records and personnel. The contract may also include an indemnification clause whereby the provider holds the insurer harmless from FCA penalties arising from the provider’s conduct.

HIPAA’s Privacy Rule (45 C.F.R. § 164.502) and Security Rule (45 C.F.R. § 164.312) govern the handling of protected health information (PHI). To operationalize these safeguards, the contract should establish a “Compliance Program” clause mandating that the provider maintain an internal compliance officer who reports quarterly to the insurer. An “Audit Rights” provision must grant the insurer the right to conduct on‑site audits of the provider’s billing practices, data security controls, and quality reporting systems. The agreement should specify that any material breach—such as a kickback scheme or HIPAA violation—constitutes grounds for immediate termination with or without notice, depending on the severity.
